sourceSnapshots.openstax:introduction-python-programming: Variables allow programs to refer to values using names rather than memory locations. A statement can set a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=). The variable name goes on the left and the value goes on the right. Note that this is different from the equal sign of mathematics, which asserts that two sides are equal; in Python the assignment statement copies the value on the right into the variable on the left. A variable name can consist of letters, digits, and underscores and be of any length. The name cannot start with a digit. Also, letter case matters, so total and Total are two different variables.

The Python interpreter uses implicit type conversion to automatically convert one data type to another, for example promoting an integer to a float in a mixed expression. A programmer can use explicit type conversion to convert one data type to another by calling a conversion function. int() converts a data type to an integer. Any fractional part is removed, so int(3.9) is 3, not 4. float() converts a data type to a float. str() converts a data type to a string, which is required before a number can be concatenated with text.

Python provides two division operators. True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float. Floor division (//) computes the quotient, or the number of times divided, discarding any remainder and returning an integer when both operands are integers. Mixing up the two is a common source of bugs when a program expects a whole number but receives a float.

An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true. If the condition is true, the body is executed. If the condition is false, the body is not executed. An else statement is used with an if statement and contains a body of statements that is executed when the if statement's condition is false. When an if-else statement is executed, one and only one of the branches is taken. The body of each branch is marked by indentation, and only the indented lines belong to the branch.

Boolean operations combine or invert conditions. The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true. The or operator takes two condition operands and returns True if either condition is true. The not operator takes one condition operand and returns True when the operand is false and returns False when the operand is true. These operators let a single if statement test compound conditions.

A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true. At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again. If true, the loop body will execute at least one more time. If false, the loop's execution will terminate. If the loop expression never becomes false, the loop never stops, producing an infinite loop, so the loop body must make progress toward ending the condition.

In Python, a container can be a range of numbers, a string of characters, or a list of values. To access objects within a container, an iterative loop can be designed to retrieve objects one at a time. A for loop iterates over all elements in a container, binding the loop variable to each element in turn. The range() function produces a sequence of integers and is commonly paired with a for loop to repeat the loop body a fixed number of times.

A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called. A function is defined using the def keyword, followed by the function name, parentheses, and a colon, with the function body indented beneath. Defining a function does not run it; the body runs only when the function is called by name. Functions let a programmer write a calculation once and reuse it many times.

A variable's scope is the part of a program where the variable can be accessed. A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function. A local variable cannot be accessed outside of the function in which the variable was created. A variable created outside of a function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program. Keeping variables local is what lets functions be reused without interfering with each other.

A list object can be used to bundle elements together in Python, holding an ordered collection of values. A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets. Individual list elements can be accessed directly using an index. Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence. An iterative for loop can be used to iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.

A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs, where each value is looked up by its key rather than by position. Since a dictionary object is used to look up values using keys, a dictionary object cannot hold duplicate key values. Dictionaries are ideal when data is naturally labeled, such as a student name mapped to a grade.

A string is made up of a sequence of characters indexed from left to right, starting at 0. For a string variable s, the left-most character is indexed 0 and the right-most character is indexed len(s) - 1. Negative indexing can also be used to refer to characters from right to left starting at -1. String slicing is used when a programmer must get access to a sequence of characters. When [a:b] is used with the name of a string variable, a sequence of characters starting from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive) is returned.

Programming often involves reading information from files and writing information into files. Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function, which returns a file object. The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string. The readline() function reads the next line in a file and returns a string. The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order. A program should close the file once it is done so the operating system can release it.

Recursion is a problem solving technique that uses the solution to a simpler version of the problem to solve the bigger problem. A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input. The recursion process continues until the problem is small enough, at which point the solution is known or can easily be found. That simplest case, solved directly without another recursive call, is the base case; without it the calls would never stop.

In a Python program, a class defines a type of object with attributes (fields) and methods (procedures). A class is a blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created of the class type are called instances. Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

misconceptions.text: Students read x = x + 1 as a mathematical equation and conclude it is impossible, instead of as an instruction to compute x + 1 and store the result back in x.
misconceptions.corrective: In Python = is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is copied into the variable on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one.

misconceptions.text: Students assume a variable stores the expression itself, so they expect it to update when the inputs later change.
misconceptions.corrective: Assignment stores the value computed at that moment; if y = x + 2 runs when x is 3, y is 5 and stays 5 even if x changes afterward.

examples.text: score = 10; score = score + 5 leaves score holding 15 — the second statement reads the old value, adds 5, and stores the new value back.

workedExamples.problem:
Trace the values of a and b after these statements run:
a = 4
b = a + 1
a = 10
What are a and b at the end?
steps: Line 1 assigns a = 4.
Line 2 evaluates the right side a + 1 with a = 4, giving 5, and stores 5 in b. b is now 5.
Line 3 reassigns a = 10. This does not re-run line 2, so b keeps the value it was already given.
workedExamples.result: a = 10 and b = 5. Reassigning a afterward does not change b, because assignment stored the computed value, not the expression.

anchor.quote: this is different from the equal sign of mathematics

misconceptions.text: Students forget to update the variable in the loop condition, so the condition stays true forever and the program hangs.

examples.text: n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1 prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops when n reaches 0.

workedExamples.problem:
Trace the output of this loop:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
steps: n = 3: check n > 0 (True), print 3, then n becomes 2.
n = 2: check n > 0 (True), print 2, then n becomes 1.
n = 1: check n > 0 (True), print 1, then n becomes 0.
n = 0: check n > 0 (False), so the loop terminates without printing.
workedExamples.result: Output: 3, 2, 1. If the body omitted n = n - 1, the condition would stay true and the loop would never end.

workedExamples.problem:

    total = price * 1.1
    return total

steps: add_tax(20) runs the body: total = 20 * 1.1 = 22.0, then returns 22.0.

misconceptions.text: Students write a recursive function with no base case, so it recurses forever and raises a RecursionError.
misconceptions.corrective: Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

misconceptions.text: Students make the recursive call on the same-size input instead of a smaller one, so it never reaches the base case.
misconceptions.corrective: Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.

examples.text: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call.

steps: factorial(3) is not the base case, so it returns 3 * factorial(2).
factorial(2) returns 2 * factorial(1); factorial(1) returns 1 * factorial(0).
factorial(0) hits the base case and returns 1. Now unwind: 1 * 1 = 1, 2 * 1 = 2, 3 * 2 = 6.
workedExamples.result: factorial(3) returns 6. The base case n == 0 stops the recursion; without it the calls would never end.

definition.text: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.

anchor.quote: In a Python program, a class defines a type of object with attributes (fields) and methods (procedures)

facts.text: A class is a blueprint for creating objects.

anchor.quote: A class is a blueprint for creating objects

facts.text: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.

anchor.quote: Individual objects created of the class type are called instances

facts.text: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

anchor.quote: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes

misconceptions.text: Students treat the class itself as an object and expect to store data on it, confusing the blueprint with the things built from it.
misconceptions.corrective: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

misconceptions.text: Students expect two instances of the same class to share their attribute values.
misconceptions.corrective: Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.

examples.text: class Dog: defines the blueprint; a = Dog() and b = Dog() are two instances, each with its own name attribute.
